name: Web Data Collection
title: Web Data Collection
answer: Web data collection in alternative data means gathering publicly available information from websites, forums, job boards, app stores, social media, and regulatory filings to build datasets that supplement traditional financial and economic data. It covers structured pages such as company career sites and product catalogs, as well as unstructured text from news, reviews, and user comments. The goal is to turn scattered online signals into time-stamped, comparable records for analysis of hiring, pricing, sentiment, product launches, and supply chain activity. This work sits inside alternative data because the sources are not standard market or accounting feeds. Practitioners treat the web as a large, continuously updated observation layer rather than a single dataset.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Web data collection in alternative data means gathering publicly available information from websites, forums, job boards, app stores, social media, and regulatory filings to build datasets that supplement traditional financial and economic data. It covers structured pages such as company career sites and product catalogs, as well as unstructured text from news, reviews, and user comments. The goal is to turn scattered online signals into time-stamped, comparable records for analysis of hiring, pricing, sentiment, product launches, and supply chain activity. This work sits inside alternative data because the sources are not standard market or accounting feeds. Practitioners treat the web as a large, continuously updated observation layer rather than a single dataset.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Collection typically runs on cloud compute with scheduled crawlers, headless browsers, and proxy networks that rotate IP addresses and manage session state. Storage is usually a mix of raw object storage for HTML and JSON, a queue or stream for newly fetched pages, and a queryable warehouse or document store for parsed records. Because sites change layout and blocking rules often, the infrastructure includes separate environments for crawling, parsing, and monitoring fetch success. Many teams keep a registry of source URLs, crawl frequency, and expected schema so that failures can be traced to a specific site or page template.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by first identifying source pages that carry a useful signal, then writing crawlers or browser scripts to fetch them on a schedule without overloading the host. Raw HTML is cleaned and parsed into fields such as job title, price, review score, or filing date, often with rules-based extractors first and machine learning models for harder text. Deduplication and entity resolution link records to companies, products, or people, and quality checks compare new extracts against known good examples. Analysts then aggregate the records into weekly or daily series, for example job postings per firm or average listed price per product.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk turn on the source's terms of service, copyright, personal data rules, and the boundary between public viewing and automated collection. Teams usually review robots.txt and site terms, avoid login-gated or paywalled content unless permission is clear, and strip or aggregate personal information before storage. Provenance matters because a price or job count is only as good as the URL, fetch time, and parser version attached to it, so records should carry source, timestamp, and extraction method. The site's own tracking of 210 compliance and regulation pages reflects how quickly rules on scraping, privacy, and data reuse are changing, and why collection programs need regular legal review.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Web data collection is moving toward more resilient extraction that can handle frequent site redesigns and anti-bot measures, with greater use of large language models to parse messy pages into clean fields. Buyers increasingly expect not just raw scrapes but documented, backtested series with clear update cadence and coverage maps. As more economic activity moves online, the value will shift from having a lot of pages to maintaining long, consistent histories for specific signals such as job posts, product availability, or app rankings. The main constraint is likely to be governance and source stability rather than the ability to fetch pages.
